questions.stem: A projectile moves through the air with no air resistance. What happens to the horizontal component of its velocity?
options: It increases steadily, because gravity speeds the projectile up
It is zero at the top of the path and largest at the ends
It stays constant, because no horizontal force acts
It decreases steadily, because gravity slows the projectile
questions.explanation: The only force is gravity, which acts vertically, so there is no horizontal acceleration and the horizontal velocity component is constant. Only the vertical component changes, by 9.80 m s⁻¹ every second.

questions.stem: At the highest point of its path, what are the velocity and acceleration of a projectile launched at 40° above the horizontal, ignoring air resistance?
options: Velocity zero; acceleration zero
Velocity horizontal and non-zero; acceleration zero
Velocity zero; acceleration 9.80 m s⁻² downward
Velocity horizontal and non-zero; acceleration 9.80 m s⁻² downward
questions.explanation: At the top the vertical velocity component is momentarily zero, but the horizontal component is unchanged, so the velocity is horizontal. Gravity still acts, so the acceleration is 9.80 m s⁻² downward throughout the flight.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked at 40 m s⁻¹ at 35° above the horizontal. What are the horizontal and vertical components of its initial velocity?
options: 20.0 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 20.0 m s⁻¹ vertical
32.8 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 22.9 m s⁻¹ vertical
22.9 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 32.8 m s⁻¹ vertical
40.0 m s⁻¹ horizontal and 0 m s⁻¹ vertical
questions.explanation: vH = v cos θ = 40 cos 35° = 32.8 m s⁻¹ and vV = v sin θ = 40 sin 35° = 22.9 m s⁻¹. Swapping sine and cosine swaps the two components.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 20.0 m high. Ignoring air resistance, how long does it take to reach the ground? Use g = 9.80 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: The vertical motion starts from zero vertical velocity: 20.0 = ½ × 9.80 × t², so t = √(40/9.80) = 2.02 s. The horizontal speed has no effect on the time to fall; dividing 20 m by 15 m s⁻¹ gives the wrong 1.33 s.

questions.stem: For the stone thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ that takes 2.02 s to fall from the cliff, how far from the base of the cliff does it land?
questions.explanation: Horizontal motion is at constant velocity, so range = vH × t = 15 × 2.02 = 30.3 m. Using twice the flight time gives 60.6 m, and dividing the speed by the time gives 7.4 m.

questions.stem: The same stone, thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹, hits the ground after 2.02 s. What is its velocity on impact? Use g = 9.80 m s⁻².
options: 19.8 m s⁻¹ straight down
24.8 m s⁻¹ at 52.9° below the horizontal
24.8 m s⁻¹ at 37.1° below the horizontal
34.8 m s⁻¹ at 52.9° below the horizontal
questions.explanation: vV = gt = 9.80 × 2.02 = 19.8 m s⁻¹ down and vH = 15 m s⁻¹. Speed = √(15² + 19.8²) = 24.8 m s⁻¹, at tan⁻¹(19.8/15) = 52.9° below the horizontal. Adding the components as numbers gives 34.8, which ignores that they are at right angles.

questions.stem: A ball is launched at 25 m s⁻¹ at 30° above level ground. Ignoring air resistance, what is its time of flight? Use g = 9.80 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: The vertical component is 25 sin 30° = 12.5 m s⁻¹. The time to reach the top is 12.5/9.80 = 1.28 s, and landing at the same height takes twice as long, 2.55 s. Using 1.28 s alone gives only the time to the top.

questions.stem: For the ball launched at 25 m s⁻¹ at 30° above level ground, what is its maximum height? Use g = 9.80 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so 0 = 12.5² − 2 × 9.80 × h and h = 156/19.6 = 7.97 m. Using the full 25 m s⁻¹ instead of the vertical component gives 31.9 m.

questions.stem: For the ball launched at 25 m s⁻¹ at 30° above level ground with a flight time of 2.55 s, what is its horizontal range?
questions.explanation: The horizontal component is 25 cos 30° = 21.7 m s⁻¹, constant throughout, so the range is 21.7 × 2.55 = 55.2 m. Multiplying the full launch speed by the time gives 63.8 m, which treats the whole velocity as horizontal.

questions.stem: For the ball launched at 25 m s⁻¹ at 30°, what is its velocity 1.0 s after launch? Use g = 9.80 m s⁻².
options: 15.2 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal
21.8 m s⁻¹ at 7.1° above the horizontal
21.7 m s⁻¹ horizontally
21.8 m s⁻¹ at 7.1° below the horizontal
questions.explanation: vH = 21.7 m s⁻¹ and vV = 12.5 − 9.80 × 1.0 = 2.7 m s⁻¹ upward, as the ball has not yet reached the top at 1.28 s. Speed = √(21.7² + 2.7²) = 21.8 m s⁻¹ at tan⁻¹(2.7/21.7) = 7.1° above the horizontal.

questions.stem: For a projectile that lands at the same height it was launched from, which launch angle gives the greatest range, ignoring air resistance?
questions.explanation: The range depends on the product of the horizontal and vertical components, which is greatest at 45°. At 90° the projectile goes straight up and lands where it started.

questions.stem: A golf ball launched at 25° above level ground lands a certain distance away. At what other angle, with the same speed, would it land at the same spot?
questions.explanation: For launches from and to the same height, complementary angles that add to 90° give the same range. 90° − 25° = 65°. The 65° shot rises higher and stays in the air longer but travels more slowly horizontally.

questions.stem: A shot-putter releases the shot about 2 m above the ground. How does the best launch angle compare with 45°?
options: It is exactly 45°, because launch height has no effect on range
It is 0°, because the shot already has height to fall from
It is less than 45°, because the shot lands below its launch height
It is more than 45°, because the shot lands below its launch height
questions.explanation: When the landing point is below the launch point, a slightly flatter launch, less than 45°, gives the greatest range, because the extra fall time already gives the shot extra horizontal travel.

questions.stem: A projectile is launched over level ground. The launch speed is doubled with the angle unchanged. Ignoring air resistance, what happens to the range?
options: It stays the same, because the angle is the same
It becomes √2 times as large
It becomes four times as large
It becomes twice as large
questions.explanation: Doubling the speed doubles both components. The time of flight doubles because the vertical component doubles, and the horizontal speed also doubles, so the range, horizontal speed × time, increases by 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.stem: One ball is dropped from a table at the same instant as an identical ball rolls off the table edge horizontally. Ignoring air resistance, which lands first?
options: The rolling ball lands first
It depends on the rolling ball's speed
Both land at the same time
The dropped ball lands first
questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration, so they fall the same height in the same time. The rolling ball simply lands further away.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a bench and lands 0.50 s later. Ignoring air resistance, how high is the bench? Use g = 9.80 m s⁻².
questions.explanation: With zero initial vertical velocity, h = ½gt² = 0.5 × 9.80 × 0.50² = 1.23 m. Forgetting the ½ gives 2.45 m.

questions.stem: A multi-image photograph of a projectile, taken at equal time intervals, shows equally spaced images horizontally but increasing spacing vertically as it falls. What does this show?
options: Decreasing horizontal velocity and constant vertical velocity
Constant horizontal velocity and increasing downward vertical velocity
Increasing horizontal velocity and constant vertical velocity
Constant horizontal acceleration and zero vertical acceleration
questions.explanation: Equal horizontal spacings in equal times mean a constant horizontal velocity. Increasing vertical spacings mean the vertical velocity is growing, because of the constant downward acceleration due to gravity.

questions.stem: In a multi-image photograph taken every 0.10 s, a ball's images are 0.25 m apart horizontally. What is the ball's horizontal velocity?
options: 25 m s⁻¹
2.5 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: vH = horizontal displacement/time interval = 0.25/0.10 = 2.5 m s⁻¹, and it is the same between every pair of images. Dividing the time by the distance gives 0.40, the reciprocal.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the drag force on a moving cyclist?
options: Riding faster, sitting more upright or riding through denser air
Riding slower, crouching lower or riding through thinner air
Riding faster, crouching lower or riding through thinner air
Riding slower, sitting more upright or riding through thinner air
questions.explanation: Drag increases with the speed of the body, the cross-sectional area it presents to the air, and the density of the medium. Sitting upright increases the area; crouching reduces it.

questions.stem: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity. What is true at that point?
options: The drag force is greater than her weight, so she slows down
The drag force is zero, because she is moving at constant speed
The drag force equals her weight, so the net force is zero
Her weight has become zero, so she no longer accelerates
questions.explanation: As her speed increases, drag increases until it equals her weight. The net force is then zero, so she stops accelerating and falls at constant terminal velocity.

questions.stem: A skydiver at terminal velocity opens her parachute. What happens next?
options: Drag exceeds her weight, so she moves upward until the drag becomes zero
Her weight increases to match the drag, so she keeps falling at the same speed
Drag becomes smaller than her weight, so she speeds up to a higher terminal velocity
Drag exceeds her weight, so she slows until a new, lower terminal velocity is reached
questions.explanation: Opening the parachute greatly increases the area, so the drag suddenly exceeds her weight and the net force is upward. She decelerates; as her speed drops, drag decreases until it again equals her weight at a much lower terminal velocity. She keeps falling downward throughout.

questions.stem: A racing car's engine force is at its maximum. Why does the car reach a top speed instead of accelerating forever?
options: The car's mass increases with speed until no further acceleration is possible
Friction from the tyres disappears at high speed, so the car cannot push
Drag rises with speed until the resistive forces equal the driving force
The engine force falls to zero once the car passes a certain speed
questions.explanation: Drag increases rapidly with speed. At top speed the total resistive force equals the maximum driving force, the net force is zero, and the car can accelerate no more. This is the car's version of terminal velocity.

questions.stem: How does air resistance change the path of a ball compared with its path in a vacuum, with the same launch speed and angle?
options: Its maximum height is reduced but its range is increased
Its range is reduced but its maximum height is unchanged
Its maximum height and range are both increased
Its maximum height and range are both reduced
questions.explanation: Drag opposes the velocity, so it reduces the horizontal component throughout the flight and adds to gravity's slowing of the vertical component on the way up. The ball rises less high and travels less far, and its path is no longer symmetrical.

questions.stem: With significant air resistance, how does the time a ball takes to rise to its maximum height compare with the time it takes to fall back down?
options: Rising and falling take exactly equal times
Rising takes no time, because it stops at once
Rising takes less time than falling
Rising takes more time than falling
questions.explanation: On the way up, drag acts downward with gravity, giving a deceleration greater than g. On the way down, drag acts upward against gravity, giving an acceleration less than g. So the ball rises quickly and falls more slowly over the same height.

questions.stem: Substituting a = Δv/Δt into F = ma, for an object of fixed mass, gives which result?
options: F = p/m, the net force equals momentum divided by mass
F = Δp/Δt, the net force equals the rate of change of momentum
F = pΔt, the net force equals momentum multiplied by time
F = Δp × m, the net force equals change in momentum times mass
questions.explanation: F = mΔv/Δt = Δ(mv)/Δt = Δp/Δt for constant mass. The net force on an object equals its rate of change of momentum, and FΔt = Δp is the impulse.

questions.stem: A 0.16 kg ball travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ is hit straight back at 30 m s⁻¹. The contact lasts 5.0 ms. What is the average force on the ball?
options: 0 N
questions.explanation: Taking the return direction as positive, Δp = 0.16 × 30 − 0.16 × (−30) = 9.6 kg m s⁻¹, so F = Δp/Δt = 9.6/0.0050 = 1.9 × 10³ N. Forgetting the reversal of direction gives Δp = 0 and no force.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg puck moving east at 4.0 m s⁻¹ is deflected so it moves north at 3.0 m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of its change in momentum?
options: 2.5 kg m s⁻¹
0.50 kg m s⁻¹
3.5 kg m s⁻¹
5.0 kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Δp = p(final) − p(initial). The initial momentum is 2.0 kg m s⁻¹ east and the final is 1.5 kg m s⁻¹ north; subtracting vectors at right angles gives |Δp| = √(2.0² + 1.5²) = 2.5 kg m s⁻¹. Subtracting the magnitudes gives 0.50, which ignores direction.

questions.stem: For the puck whose momentum changes from 2.0 kg m s⁻¹ east to 1.5 kg m s⁻¹ north, in which direction did the average force on it act?
options: About 53° south of east
Due north
About 37° north of west
About 37° north of east
questions.explanation: The force acts in the direction of Δp = p(final) + (−p(initial)), which is 1.5 north plus 2.0 west. That points tan⁻¹(1.5/2.0) ≈ 37° north of west.

questions.stem: A ball's momentum of 3.0 kg m s⁻¹ is turned through 60° with no change in magnitude. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum?
options: 3.0 kg m s⁻¹
0 kg m s⁻¹
6.0 kg m s⁻¹
1.5 kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: The initial momentum, final momentum and Δp form a triangle with two sides of 3.0 and a 60° angle between them, which is equilateral. So |Δp| = 3.0 kg m s⁻¹. The momentum's magnitude is unchanged, but its direction has changed, so Δp is not zero.

questions.stem: A ball strikes a smooth wall at an angle and rebounds at the same speed and angle. In which direction does the wall push the ball?
options: Along the ball's outgoing direction of travel
Perpendicular to the wall, away from it
Parallel to the wall, along the ball's motion
Along the ball's incoming direction of travel
questions.explanation: The velocity component parallel to the wall is unchanged and the perpendicular component reverses, so Δp, and hence the force, is perpendicular to the wall and directed away from it.

questions.stem: Using Newton's third law, why is momentum conserved when two particles interact in an isolated system?
options: They exert forces in the same direction, so their momenta both increase
The heavier particle exerts the larger force, so it loses all its momentum
No forces act between the particles, so neither momentum can change
They exert equal and opposite forces for the same time, so Δp₁ = −Δp₂
questions.explanation: F₁ = −F₂ and the forces act for the same time Δt, so F₁Δt = −F₂Δt, giving Δp₁ = −Δp₂. Whatever momentum one particle gains, the other loses, so the total is unchanged.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg puck moving east at 5.0 m s⁻¹ strikes an identical stationary puck on frictionless ice. Afterwards the first puck moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹, 37° north of east. What is the second puck's velocity?
options: 3.0 m s⁻¹, 53° south of east
3.0 m s⁻¹, 53° north of east
1.0 m s⁻¹, due east
5.0 m s⁻¹, 37° south of east
questions.explanation: Total momentum is 10 kg m s⁻¹ east. The first puck has 8.0 kg m s⁻¹ at 37° north of east, and the second must supply the rest: a right-angled triangle with sides 10, 8.0 and 6.0, so the second has 6.0 kg m s⁻¹, or 3.0 m s⁻¹, at 53° south of east. Subtracting speeds gives 1.0 m s⁻¹, which ignores direction.

questions.stem: A stationary 4.0 kg object explodes into three pieces. A 1.0 kg piece moves east at 12 m s⁻¹ and another 1.0 kg piece moves north at 9.0 m s⁻¹. What is the velocity of the 2.0 kg third piece?
options: 10.5 m s⁻¹, due south-west
7.5 m s⁻¹, 37° south of west
7.5 m s⁻¹, 37° north of east
15 m s⁻¹, 37° south of west
questions.explanation: The total momentum stays zero, so the third piece's momentum cancels the vector sum of 12 kg m s⁻¹ east and 9.0 kg m s⁻¹ north, which is 15 kg m s⁻¹. It moves the opposite way, at tan⁻¹(9/12) ≈ 37° south of west, with speed 15/2.0 = 7.5 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: In a multi-image photograph, a puck of mass m moves 6 grid squares between images. It hits and sticks to a stationary puck of mass 2m. How many squares do they move between images afterwards?
questions.explanation: The spacing between images is proportional to speed, since the flash rate is constant. Momentum is conserved: m × 6 = 3m × v, so v corresponds to 2 squares per interval. Sharing between two pucks as if they had equal mass gives 3.

questions.stem: How does a spacecraft gain momentum by emitting gas from its thrusters?
options: The gas pushes on the surrounding space, which pushes the spacecraft forward
The gas loses momentum backward, so the spacecraft must lose momentum too
The gas makes the spacecraft lighter, which by itself makes it move faster
The gas gains momentum backward, so the spacecraft gains equal momentum forward
questions.explanation: The spacecraft and gas form an isolated system with constant total momentum. When gas is pushed backward with some momentum, the spacecraft gains an equal momentum forward. There is nothing in space to push against.

questions.stem: An ion thruster ejects xenon ions at 3.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹, emitting 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ kg of ions each second. What thrust does it produce?
questions.explanation: Thrust = rate of change of momentum of the ions = (Δm/Δt) × v = 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 3.0 × 10⁴ = 0.090 N. The thrust is tiny, but the very high exhaust speed means little fuel is needed, so it can run for months and build up a large speed.

questions.stem: A solar sail can accelerate a spacecraft without fuel. What makes this possible?
options: Photons carry mass, which is added to the sail when they strike it
Sunlight heats the sail, and the hot sail pushes against the vacuum
The solar wind's gravity pulls the sail away from the Sun
Photons carry momentum, which is transferred to the sail when they strike it
questions.explanation: Although photons have no mass, they carry momentum, p = h/λ. When photons strike the sail their momentum changes, so they exert a force on it and the sail gains momentum.

questions.stem: Identical streams of photons strike two sails at right angles. One sail reflects them and the other absorbs them. How do the accelerations compare, for sails of equal mass?
options: The reflecting sail does not accelerate, because the photons bounce off
The reflecting sail's acceleration is twice the absorbing sail's
The absorbing sail's acceleration is twice the reflecting sail's
Both accelerations are equal, because the same photons arrive
questions.explanation: An absorbed photon's momentum changes from p to zero, so Δp = p. A reflected photon's momentum changes from p to −p, so Δp = 2p. The sail gains twice the momentum per photon from reflection, so it has twice the force and acceleration.
